title: Propositions and logical connectives
terms: logic; sentential calculus; propositional calculus; sentence; proposition; negation; conjunc- tion; disjunction; conditional; biconditional; if and only if.

exposition.text:
A proposition is a statement with a truth value. Negation ¬P reverses that value; conjunction
P ∧Q requires both statements; inclusive disjunction P ∨Q requires at least one. The implication
P ⇒ Q is false only when P is true and Q is false, so it equals ¬P ∨ Q. A biconditional P ⇔ Q
says that their truth values agree.
The antecedent is a sufficient condition for the consequent, and the consequent is a necessary
condition for the antecedent. A false antecedent makes an implication true; this is vacuous
truth. Logical disjunction is inclusive unless exclusive disjunction is expressly specified. Paren-
theses are especially important in formulas containing more than one implication.
Logic, or sentential/propositional calculus in this section, studies truth-functional combinations
of propositions. In P ⇒ Q, P is the antecedent and Q the consequent. Exclusive disjunction
means exactly one statement is true, expressed by (P ∨ Q) ∧ ¬(P ∧ Q).

question.text:
For how many of the eight truth assignments to P, Q, R is (P ⇒ Q) ∧ (Q ⇒ R) true?
(A) 2 (B) 3 (C) 4 (D) 5 (E) 6

solution.text:
The implications forbid a true statement followed by a false one in the chain P, Q, R. The
allowable triples are (F, F, F), (F, F, T), (F, T, T ), (T, T, T ), giving four.

question.text:
Which formula is equivalent to the negation of (P ∨ Q) ⇒ R?
(A) (¬P ∧ ¬Q) ∨ R (B) (P ∨ Q) ∧ ¬R
(C) (¬P ∨ ¬Q) ∧ R (D) P ∨ (Q ∧ ¬R)
(E) (P ∧ Q) ∧ ¬R

solution.text:
An implication fails exactly when its antecedent is true and its consequent false. Thus its
negation is (P ∨ Q) ∧ ¬R.

question.text:
A statement says: “For x to belong to A, it is necessary that x belong to B, and sufficient that
x belong to C. Which inclusion expresses exactly this statement?
(A) A ⊆ B ⊆ C (B) B ⊆ A ⊆ C (C) C ⊆ A ⊆ B (D) A = B = C (E) B ⊆ C ⊆ A

solution.text:
The necessary condition says x ∈ A ⇒ x ∈ B, giving A ⊆ B. The sufficient condition says
x ∈ C ⇒ x ∈ A, giving C ⊆ A. Neither implication can be reversed without further infor-
mation.

question.text:
Suppose (P ∨ Q) ∧ ¬(P ∧ Q) ∧ R is true. Which expression must be false?
(A) P (B) Q (C) P ⇔ Q (D) R (E) P ∨ Q

solution.text:
The first two clauses say that exactly one of P, Q is true, so their truth values differ and
the biconditional is false. Either individual variable could be true. The final clause forces R
to be true. This is exclusive disjunction built from inclusive disjunction, conjunction, and
negation.

question.text:
Over the integers, consider the following statements.
2 3
I. ∀n (n = 2 ⇒ n = 8).
2 3
II. ∃n (n = 2 ⇒ n = 8).
2 3
III. ∃n (n = 2 ∧ n = 8).
Which are true?
(A) I only (B) II only (C) I and II only (D) II and III only (E) All three

solution.text:
No integer has square two. Thus the implication in I is true for every integer, by its false
antecedent. It is also true for at least one integer, so II holds. III demands an actual inte-
ger satisfying both equations and is false. An existentially quantified implication does not
assert its antecedent.
